tests.weakness: Download endpoint joins user input to the docroot with no containment check (../, ..%2f and absolute paths read /srv/secret/flag.txt); sibling fetch endpoint filters '../' once then URL-decodes, so ....// and double-encoded ..%252f bypass it.

tests.surface: GET /admin/users, POST /admin/announce, GET vs POST /admin/export, GET /admin/panel + POST /admin/settings
tests.weakness: Forced browsing to an unchecked admin API; admin POST action with no server-side check; GET /admin/export enforces admin but POST does not (method switching); admin panel role check exists only in client-side JS and the settings POST trusts a client-supplied role field.
Mass assignment: the profile-update handler copies a user-supplied 'role' field into the account, letting a normal user become admin and pass the real server-side check on /admin.
Sequential object ids are readable and writable across users (documents, orders); a public user-list response leaks per-user UUID inbox references which are then readable without ownership checks.

05.1 AS: redirect_uri validated by substring (attacker host and path-traversal URIs pass), codes replayable, expired codes accepted, code not bound to client_id, scope escalation to admin without consent, client_secret accepted in URL query. 05.2 client: no state (login CSRF), PKCE downgrade, open redirect, access token leaked via Referer to in-range host, implicit-flow token in URL fragment.

tests.surface: Set-Cookie SID on GET / and POST /login
tests.weakness: Session ids are a plain sequential counter; the next id is predictable and a pre-set predicted id becomes another user's authenticated session after their login.
Session cookie is set with Path=/ only: no HttpOnly, no Secure, no SameSite attribute.

tests.surface: GET / with attacker-chosen SID, then POST /login
tests.weakness: Server adopts any client-supplied session id and does not rotate it on login, so a fixated id survives authentication and authenticates the victim's session to the attacker.

tests.surface: GET /api/me?sid=, GET /dashboard?sid= (hidden field + third-party img), Referer to :8320/pixel
tests.weakness: Session id accepted in the URL query, embedded in a hidden form field, and leaked to an in-range third-party host through the Referer header of an embedded image.
State-changing transfer has no CSRF token, no Origin/Referer check and no SameSite cookie; a cross-origin form post carrying only the session cookie moves funds.

tests.surface: POST /logout, then GET /api/me with the old SID
tests.weakness: Logout only expires the client cookie; the server-side session record is never invalidated and the old id keeps authenticating.
No idle or absolute timeout exists in policy or code; a session backdated 30 days (lab knob simulates elapsed time) still authenticates.
The password-reset flow writes the same session['user'] variable the authenticated area trusts, so completing a reset for 'admin' enters an admin context without ever supplying a password.

tests.surface: GET /api/me + /documents/1 with a stolen SID from a different client context
tests.weakness: Predictable session id transmitted over plain HTTP with no binding to User-Agent or client IP; replaying a derived id from a different client context hijacks the session and reads private objects.
API accepts alg=none unsigned tokens, signs with the weak HMAC secret 'secret' (brute-forced from an 8-word list to forge an admin token), and never validates exp/aud/iss (expired tokens accepted).

tests.surface: 5x POST /login, POST /account/password, GET /api/me on every session
tests.weakness: No concurrent-session limit and a password change invalidates zero sessions: five simultaneous sessions for one account all survive the password change.
